name: Diamond-Blackfan Anaemia
aliases: pure red cell aplasia of infancy

clinicalPearls: An inherited pure red cell aplasia that typically presents in early infancy, usually within the first year of life, with macrocytic anaemia and reticulocytopenia while white cells and platelets are preserved.
It is a ribosomopathy caused by mutations in ribosomal protein genes, of which RPS19 is the most common; inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, and many cases arise de novo.
Raised erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity and raised fetal haemoglobin support the diagnosis and help distinguish it from acquired red cell aplasia.

Congenital anomalies occur in around half of patients, notably thumb and radial-ray defects (including triphalangeal thumb), craniofacial dysmorphism, short stature, and cardiac and genitourinary malformations.
Corticosteroids are the mainstay of initial treatment and produce a response in many children, though steroid dependence or transfusion dependence is common.
Regular transfusion with iron chelation is used for steroid-refractory disease, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative option for the marrow failure.
There is a lifelong predisposition to malignancy, particularly myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukaemia, osteosarcoma and certain other solid tumours.
It must be distinguished from transient erythroblastopenia of childhood, which occurs in older children, is normocytic and self-limiting, and shows normal erythrocyte adenosine deaminase.
reference.pathophysiology: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding proteins of the small or large ribosomal subunit, leading to haploinsufficiency and defective ribosomal RNA processing and ribosome assembly. This impaired ribosome biogenesis generates nucleolar stress that stabilises and activates the p53 tumour-suppressor pathway, driving cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis. Erythroid progenitors are uniquely sensitive to this stress, producing a selective failure of red cell production with sparing of the other lineages. Rare cases involve mutations affecting the erythroid transcription factor pathway, such as GATA1, which impair erythroid-specific translation and give a comparable phenotype. The same disturbance of ribosomal function and p53 signalling is thought to underlie the associated congenital malformations, growth impairment and heightened cancer predisposition.
additionalDifferentials: Parvovirus B19-induced red cell aplasia (especially with underlying haemolysis)
Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (Fanconi anaemia, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film showing macrocytosis
Bone marrow examination demonstrating selective erythroid hypoplasia with preserved myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages
Targeted genetic testing of ribosomal protein and related genes
Echocardiography, renal ultrasound and skeletal assessment for associated anomalies
Parvovirus B19 studies to exclude an acquired cause
redFlags: New cytopenias in other lineages or marrow dysplasia suggesting transformation to myelodysplasia or leukaemia
Bone pain, swelling or a mass raising concern for osteosarcoma
Features of transfusional iron overload affecting the heart, liver or endocrine organs
Severe anaemia with signs of cardiac compromise
Failure to respond to, or loss of response to, established therapy
reference.prognosis: With corticosteroids and transfusion support many patients survive into adulthood, but long-term morbidity arises from iron overload, treatment toxicity and malignancy; stem cell transplantation can cure the marrow failure though it does not remove the underlying cancer predisposition.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with transient erythroblastopenia of childhood and delaying diagnosis; age, red cell size and erythrocyte adenosine deaminase help differentiate them.
Overlooking subtle radial-ray or thumb anomalies that point to the diagnosis.
Under-monitoring and under-treating transfusional iron overload.
Exposing a growing infant to prolonged high-intensity corticosteroid therapy without weighing growth and toxicity effects.
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood (standard reference)
British Society for Haematology guidance (standard reference)
management: Initiate corticosteroids as the mainstay of first-line treatment, which produce a response in many children
Support steroid-refractory or steroid-dependent disease with regular red cell transfusion
Add iron chelation therapy to manage transfusional iron overload
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative therapy for the marrow failure
Screen for and manage associated anomalies with echocardiography, renal imaging and skeletal review, and monitor growth
Surveil for treatment toxicity and the lifelong increased risk of myelodysplasia, leukaemia and solid tumours
Offer genetic counselling and family screening, as inheritance is usually autosomal dominant with frequent de novo variants
